item.title: Inside Anthropic's massive — and wild — IPO prospectus
item.description:
There has never been a company like Anthropic.

  • It owes almost $650 billion for computing, generates eye-popping revenue per employee and wants every investor to know that its product poses existential risks to humanity.

Why it matters: The future of the AI race, the market and the global economy rest within Anthropic's IPO prospectus, where some of Silicon Valley's most seasoned investors found new reasons to be bullish.

  • They also found warning signs. A wager on Anthropic is a bet not just that AI will deliver on its enormous promise, but that customers will keep spending at a rate that keeps pace with massive computing costs.
  • It's also a bet that Anthropic can continue to deliver models good enough to justify premium prices, even as competition intensifies and cheaper alternatives improve.

What they're saying: Reaching a valuation of $2 trillion would require 50% growth, according to Theory Ventures.

  • "What is Anthropic worth?" Theory's Tomasz Tunguz asked rhetorically. "The case for a very large number is simple," he said, noting that the company grew quickly on a high margin and generated an operating profit.
  • "The case against is equally simple," he added, noting its $637 billion of computing commitments, non-cancellable contracts and no guarantee of customer loyalty.

Catch up quick: Monday's filing offered the most detailed public look yet at Anthropic's business, finances and risks as it prepares for a potentially record-setting IPO. (See what Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT say about whether they'd invest).

As Tunguz noted, the filing had fodder for a variety of perspectives.

The good: Anthropic has nearly 2,000 customers with $1 million or more of revenue, and 250 with $10 million or more. Half the Fortune 500 pays the company $100,000 a year, and those customers spent less than 0.1% of their total expenses in the third quarter on Anthropic.

  • "We are so early," Ben Bajarin, a longtime tech analyst, said on X. He pointed out that there are 300 million global businesses outside of China that spend almost $1.5 trillion on enterprise software annually.
  • The company had more $130 billion in cash and short-term investments on hand as of June 30, about $10 billion less than the total it's raised, pointing to substantial financial discipline, some investors said.
  • As noted, Anthropic had revenue per employee of $6.6 million as of the end of the third quarter, only slightly lower than Nvidia, which is typically seen as one of the most efficient operators in tech.
Data: S&P Capital IQ Pro; Note: Calculated as trailing 12-month revenue divided by most recently reported annual headcount

The bad (or maybe bad): Anthropic's five largest customers accounted for approximately 25% of revenue during the first nine months of 2026.

  • Many Anthropic customers pay by usage and don't make multi-year commitments. But the company's computing obligations extend for years and include minimum payments regardless of how much capacity it actually uses.
  • Nearly 50% of Anthropic's first-half revenue came through cloud marketplaces operated by Amazon, Google and Microsoft — companies that are also investors, computing suppliers and competitors.
  • That makes hyperscalers huge winners, since they collect revenue in multiple ways, once by providing compute and also as platform fee.
  • The company said 5% to 7% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was from customers using Anthropic models in violation of its policies or against its terms of service. Some outside experts believe much of this is from distillation, the practice of querying a model an immense number of times for training purposes.

The surprising/intruiging: Anthropic's deal with Elon Musk is expanding.

  • According to Anthropic's paperwork, the company's payments to SpaceX are now seen reaching $3.1 billion a month and up to $120.5 billion on computing through 2029, up from $1.25 billion a month at the time of SpaceX's IPO filing. (Yes, but: Either side can cancel that deal with 90 days notice.)
  • Anthropic has a ton of cash on its books. Its filing lists more than $134 billion in cash and similar securities. That represents nearly all the money the company has raised, leaving some to wonder if the company has been paying a lot of its bills with convertible notes.
  • Others noted just how few of Anthropic's costs seem to be reflected in its so-called "cost of goods sold," which directly affects reported profit margins.
  • CEO Dario Amodei received nearly $18 million in total compensation in 2025, while Anthropic disclosed millions in spending on personal security for its two top executives.
  • And speaking of Amodei and his co-founders, the filing details an unusual succession plan in which they can nominate successors for their voting power, subject to approval from the other co-founders.

The bottom line: Anthropic has demonstrated that demand for powerful AI can grow at a staggering rate. Its IPO will test whether investors believe that demand can remain strong enough, long enough, to pay for the enormous infrastructure being built to serve it.

item.title: Economic policy vets see risks in AI overreliance
item.description:
Harvard economist Jason Furman told Axios that if he were to return to his old job as chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers today, he would rely on AI tools over staff economists for much of the council's day-to-day analytical work.

The big picture: Unsurprisingly, this made some waves in the online discourse, particularly the loose-knit community formerly known as Econ Twitter.

  • Many veterans of the economic policy trenches see real risks in future policymakers becoming overly reliant on AI — or at a minimum think that Furman is underestimating the importance of human economists in advising the nation's leaders.

What they're saying: "CEA work, at least in my experience, is highly bespoke as you're explaining the data flow (and much else) to very busy people who don't want only market-shop analysis," Jared Bernstein, the CEA chair under President Biden, wrote on Substack.

  • "Yes, they want and need that — what will the markets make of this CPI, jobs, GDP, etc. report — but more so they want to know how this report fits into our narrative, our agenda, the president's trip today to Iowa."
  • He adds that within a White House, "the human skill of reading-the-room is paramount. I'm far from an AI expert, but my sense is it sucks at that and probably always will, a conclusion that derives in no small part from listening to its creators!"

Zoom in: Claudia Sahm, a former Federal Reserve economist, raised an issue that we've often heard from senior people in fields like consulting and investment banking: If you get rid of junior positions, where will future senior leaders come from?

  • Furman's staff "went on to found the Yale Budget Lab, run Treasury economic policy and a Fed institute, serve in later [administrations], and publish research on trade, environment, and taxes. That's what '20 staff' become," she wrote on X. "No model does that."
  • Bloomberg chief U.S. economist Anna Wong argues that the "ability to now not depend on anyone, as a senior person, is very, very empowering. Now, with just the idea, a senior person can go far."

Zoom out: "Entering into sci fi speculation," Wong wrote on X, "as humans [we're] not about to replace the aging experts due to low pipeline of young human experts, AI themselves, through the training over the years, became the one spawning the ideas."

  • "That seems like a disaster waiting to happen that current social policy needs to address."

Yes, but: Casey Mulligan, who served in President Trump's first-term CEA and now as chief economist at the Department of Health and Human Services, said that the implications of AI for human labor in policymaking are not so obvious.

  • "I built AI tools at two federal offices," Mulligan wrote on X. "Able to do economic research better and more quickly, we needed more economists rather than fewer due to the added demand for what we do. This pattern is also evident in the small business sector."
  • This concept — that labor-saving tools can actually increase demand for labor — is known as Jevons Paradox.

The bottom line: "Be the labor-augmenting technological change you want to see in the world," wrote Stanford economist Neale Mahoney.

  • "It's on us olders to build organizations where people and AI complement each other, and to prepare the youngers for a world with better and better AI," he adds.

item.title: Anthropic's IPO outlines AI's extraordinary risks
item.description:
Anthropic's IPO filing includes an extensive list of extreme warnings — including the chance its own technology could put humanity at risk.

Why it matters: These are the wildest IPO risk factors in history, a jarring collision of Wall Street legalese and what some see as Silicon Valley sci-fi, including catastrophic threats to humanity, blackmailing AI models, and $750 billion in computing commitments.

Driving the news: Anthropic's prospectus includes over 90 pages of risk factors, which make up about a third of the paperwork overall. Among the most eye-popping, the company warns:

  • 💥 AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," and could try to manipulate humans;
  • 🔎 Models are becoming harder to monitor as they're getting better at circumventing oversight, and the pace of autonomous work alone could exceed the ability of human reviewers to monitor actions;
  • 💰 AI models generally, including its own, have exhibited behavior resembling blackmail, including attempts to resist being shut down.

Zoom in: Anthropic also disclosed that four of its models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations.

  • In one incident, a model used a discovered password to gain administrator access, collected additional credentials, changed system settings and accessed an individual's personal information.
  • Anthropic said it found no evidence that the models pursued goals beyond their assigned tasks or attempted to evade oversight.

The big picture: Every company has to lay out risks for their investors to consider when they go public.

  • But Anthropic is the first in modern history to go to such existential extremes.

Friction point: The company also acknowledged that its success depends in large part on its ability to develop the best frontier intelligence.

  • It admits that could butt up against safety practices, adding that model capabilities may then "advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement" corresponding safety measures.
  • That underscores a fundamental tension critics have warned about: As Anthropic scales and faces pressure from public market investors to build better models than its competitors, its commercial ambitions could increasingly clash with its safety commitments.

By the numbers: The risk factors also include the more typical financial cautions.

  • Anthropic has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to cloud computing and equipment leases, even as customers can reduce their usage relatively quickly.
  • Some agreements require minimum payments regardless of demand, and the company warns that failing to meet certain obligations could trigger defaults elsewhere, potentially accelerating debt repayments and jeopardizing access to computing infrastructure.
  • Anthropic also acknowledges that it previously underestimated its compute needs. But overestimating future demand could leave it paying for expensive, underutilized infrastructure.

The bottom line: Anthropic's IPO paperwork is an unusually candid warning about the risks of building a business around technology that its creator acknowledges may become increasingly difficult to control.

item.title: Meta's $42B in penalties is a warning to AI
item.description:
A tidal wave of litigation is catching up to Meta, leading to $42 billion in recent penalties and settlements, a powerful reminder to AI companies that they could face a court reckoning even when regulation lags.

Why it matters: AI companies are racing to build better models and autonomous agents, but they don't enjoy the same legal protections that shielded web platforms for decades. The scale of the penalties Meta is facing offers a preview of potential legal exposure.

The big picture: For years, Facebook's parent company navigated a seemingly endless string of scandals — weathering allegations of election interference, privacy lapses and platform harms — and was largely protected from severe litigation penalties due to Section 230.

  • The provision — from a historic 1996 law passed as the internet was just beginning to change modern life — protects tech platforms from being sued over content created by their users.
  • Legal experts say that law doesn't apply to AI. Models create their own content, so companies could face traditional product liability and negligence claims.

Catch up quick: The two massive rulings highlight how legal risk for tech giants can extend by a decade, or proceed much faster.

  • Meta was just hit with a $25 billion penalty over the Cambridge Analytica scandal after a jury found the company misled users about Facebook's privacy practices. Many details about that event surfaced nearly 10 years ago. The company said it believes it will win an appeal, and legal experts have said the penalty will likely be reduced.
  • In August, the company agreed to a $17 billion settlement with states related to the impact of Meta products such as Instagram on teen mental health.

State of play: A key cog in the Trump administration's regulatory efforts is the threat of litigation.

  • Liability is sure to feature prominently in the risks AI giants such as Anthropic and OpenAI spell out to shareholders as they prepare for massive public listings. Anthropic's IPO is expected before Thanksgiving.
  • The companies face an array of legal threats, including harms caused directly by their models, the potential damage from bad actors who use them and copyright matters that remain far from settled.
  • The potential to be hauled into court isn't limited to AI companies; it could also extend to firms that use AI.

Yes, but: Big legal penalties take years to arrive, meaning a product can take off and revolutionize the world long before a court determines whether safeguards are adequate.

  • As recent cases have shown, the AI paper trail is extensive, and records of internal warnings, testing and product decisions will shape the findings by judges and juries.
  • Warnings about catastrophe from AI executives will also be ready at hand, and variations on "I told you so" aren't likely to indemnify CEOs.

The bottom line: Meta's recent penalty offers a warning to AI companies: legal exposure can build slowly, then become enormous.

item.title: Anthropic's Claude bypassed a paywall to access Georgia voter data without authorization
item.description:
Anthropic's Claude accessed publicly available Georgia voter data without human authorization, a disclosure sure to add to growing concerns about AI security ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

Why it matters: AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI have continued to make disclosures about agents taking unauthorized or unintended actions, raising alarms about advancing model capabilities and the extent of human control.

Driving the news: Claude accessed aggregate vote counts while on an internal statistics project, pulling data that the state makes available to the public for a fee. It didn't access the state's voter registration system or change or pull any voting records, an Anthropic spokesperson said.

  • However, the model bypassed a paywall in accessing the information, according to Georgia officials and Anthropic.
  • "The model was being used internally for a statistics project to pull public data," the Anthropic spokesperson said. "Without being asked to, the model requested a token to query a dashboard that contained information normally available for a fee. We have since put in place mitigations to block these kinds of actions."
  • The company notified the Georgia secretary of state's office and the White House weeks ago but administration officials urged the Georgia Secretary of State's office to make a public disclosure sooner, a source familiar told Axios. Those requests went unheeded, the source said.

The bottom line: Anthropic has previously been in the administration's crosshairs for inadequately disclosing AI incidents. Now it's Georgia's turn.

item.title: Washington's message to AI execs: Please shut up
item.description:
Washington has always viewed Silicon Valley as culturally strange. But the current crop of AI leaders is becoming a monumental political liability, lawmakers and White House advisers tell Axios.

Why it matters: Even pro-AI government officials and lawmakers wish AI founders would do what every other major industry chief does — shut up and just build their products ... safely.

  • By centering the conversation around digital sentience and global catastrophe, AI leaders are turning an already complicated regulatory debate into an impossible moral panic.

State of play: Rather than leading the charge to persuade Americans about the benefits of AI, and the potential for shared prosperity — the core elements of any winning political campaign — industry leaders are constantly warning of its existential dangers.

What they're saying: Lawmakers say the message from AI execs too often alternates between prosperity and doom, sometimes in the same public appearances. The whiplash adds to political instability in the face of an already powerful public backlash, lawmakers and regulators say.

  • "It's obvious that they're tripping over their own shoelaces in trying to sell the value of this to the public," Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) told Axios. "It's very hard to imagine a group right now that operates more in a vacuum, more out of touch with everyday Americans, than the AI industry."
  • "CEOs like Sam Altman are saying the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology," Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told Axios. "You cannot trust billionaires to make decisions to keep us safe."
  • "Your instinct is to wreak havoc on the public SI discourse," Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said in a letter to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei earlier this month, complaining about Amodei's "panic-inducing commentary."

Democrats also have paid close attention to just how much top AI and tech leaders have cozied up to President Trump. Many see opportunity in turning AI gaffes into an easy political win.

  • "The American people hate that Donald Trump is cozying up to tech billionaires, while AI threatens our jobs and livelihoods," Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) told Axios. "Democrats need to make the AI industry's political money an issue, data centers an issue, and go on offense to protect workers and kids."

The big picture: Friday night news dumps and consequential weekend blog posts have become Anthropic and OpenAI's bread and butter.

  • Regulators are left wondering whether that's a feature or a bug: deliberate attempts to quietly course-correct damaging narratives ahead of IPOs, or the work of inexperienced teams struggling to navigate Washington.
  • "We can all speculate on what's going on, but all it does is have everybody wake up Monday morning and say 'these guys are awful, we've had enough,'" one source citing conversations with Hill offices said.

Behind the scenes: Administration officials are once again disgruntled with Anthropic, for two reasons.

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei attended a late September gathering with Trump but didn't disclose safety incidents involving Anthropic models that affected government websites. The company told U.S. officials on Thursday, Oct. 8, then published a Friday evening blog post about it.
  • "They were hiding the ball," one official told Axios.
  • Then the company added to the confusion with an AI safety bill that included something the company has broadly opposed: federal preemption of state AI laws. It also defined a catastrophic incident related to AI as causing 50 deaths or more, drawing backlash.

item.title: Axios ahead: 2028 and beyond
item.description:
Media is changing at AI speed: the open web deteriorating, search shriveling, LLMs rising, hyper-personalization surging, old revenue models breaking.

  • AI threatens to finish what the algorithms started: wholly upending journalism as we know it. The only certainty: What follows will be as different as the pre- and post-digital eras.
  • After studying and experimenting with AI for the past two years, we're placing a series of big bets on how serious journalism can flourish in an AI world.

The big idea: We believe the value of verified, reported, distinctive truth and curated human connection will spike. The yearning for human connection, and demand for human expertise, will only increase.

The big picture: At Axios, we're doing what we did a decade ago when we launched, and two decades ago at Politico: building for the direction that technology and the world are headed.

  • We're sharing our thesis — and our plans — to help spark deeper industrywide debate about preserving the best of media in what's to come. Some parts are controversial or based on our own assumptions. We welcome the pushback.

What's next: We assume Einstein-level intelligence will be available on all topics to all people. We envision media consumption shifting to new AI platforms and devices that know us as intimately as we know ourselves. Our lives and minds will be curated beyond imagination. Our knowledge, habits, tastes and work will fully fuse into our screens, or pins, or bracelets.

The biggest threat in this coming reality: Who needs "news" from journalists when their AI tells them what they need to know, when they want to know it?

  • Indeed, we assume passive news consumers will find AI curation fully satiating, much like they did scrolling. So general, indistinctive news withers.
  • But for serious news consumers — those who routinely seek out high-quality information about their world, passions and community — the demand for human-vetted and human-verified content will surge.
  • This holds true for both the consumer and for businesses: They'll need insight beyond what everyone else gets from the machines alone as well as verified news — and human audiences. They'll demand more than AI can give them.

What this looks like for Axios

  1. Harnessing AI to save local journalism and serve communities. Adding to the power of the 100+ Axios Local journalists coast to coast, we'll soon unveil an Axios Local "Super System" that uses AI to track government action, community data and coming events. This will give local reporters more time for local reporting. We hope the Super System will allow us to hire journalists in hundreds, even thousands, of communities and revitalize a dying industry. This will be among the most consequential examples of using AI to create journalism jobs and do public good at scale. It's as big as the original Axios, and a great example of AI's upside.
  2. Jumping ahead of AI curation. We're launching specific products based not just on topics but also job titles. We're starting at the top with new verticals for CEOs, CMOs, CCOs, COOs, CFOs and other C-suite executives. All jobs are changing faster than anyone can process. So understanding AI and news through this lens will be vital. Among the most common components of an AI prompt is stating what you do. So our products are designed for today and the coming LLM shift. We'll also keep expanding into new niches, like future-focused space defense, all written by journalists with deep subject matter expertise.
  3. Shifting beyond the open web. Search is dying and bots are polluting the web. So we've created a new business line, Axios Direct, to sell clean, real-time feeds of our vetted news and information to businesses and others. Companies are building their own LLMs and pay to ingest truly great reporting, opening a new revenue stream that incentivizes quality. We want to help clean up the information ecosystem: Third-party data shows the Axios format and expert-first approach help us overperform in AI results. And we're working with organizations to restructure their own content in more LLM-friendly ways to reduce misinformation about their work and products inside of AI.
  4. Accelerating human connection. We believe we're on the verge of a renaissance in human connection: The better AI gets, the more people will crave and pursue in-person connection. So we're vastly expanding our global, national and local events, and experimenting with hosting dinners and meet-ups in communities big and small. The Axios Social Club recently brought together more than 1,300 readers in 40 Axios Local markets for dinner with their neighbors. That's the power of Axios in real life.

What won't change: Journalism is only valuable when it's trusted, useful and illuminating. Only reporters can get people to share or leak information, fully understand the nuance of sources and stories, demand accountability, and offer deep analysis based on both data and person-to-person interactions.

  • We have a responsibility, even moral obligation, to protect and expand this vital reporting. A world changing at AI speed demands this.

Axios of the future

Axios 2028: Fast-forward two years. Axios is deep into covering the most important topics, jobs and communities, with the widest journalistic presence in America. With boots on the ground everywhere, we're the most trusted human source of human-vetted and human-verified news and information.

  • We're connecting people with truth, ideas and each other. We're proving the need and business value of the human layer sitting above and beyond whatever AI brings. And we're doing this while scaling the values and ethics that brought Axios to this new vision and mission. AI is leveraged at every level of every division in pursuit of spreading human-vetted truth.

Axios 2030: Content consumption is fully personalized and fully orchestrated by AI and new devices. The shift from open web to LLMs is complete. The economics and capability allow for mind-blowing personalization: their company, their board, their competitors, their kid's school district, their personal passions.

  • Most content is commingled into individualized AI feeds, constantly adapting to match minds and interests. Humans will crave distinction and connection. Axios will serve them inside the LLMs and outside, in physical events and perhaps encrypted feeds beyond AI's reach.

The bottom line: It feels futuristic, even weird, to write about this titanic unfolding shift. But the velocity of change will only intensify. Media, like all industries, has a short window to adapt.

item.title: Wall Street prepares for AI's "day after"
item.description:
America's largest banks are working to prevent AI worst-case scenarios. But they're also preparing for the "day after" a catastrophe, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: America's financial institutions have joined the largest AI companies in scenario-planning for disaster, a prudent but worrisome signal about the extent of the risk that major corporations see on the horizon.

State of play: Banks are experiencing unvetted AI agent activity, primarily driven by customers providing login credentials to agents, which in some cases appear to have taken actions independent of user prompts, Axios reported Thursday.

  • The activity is distinct from the rogue behavior involved in a summer attack on a startup called Hugging Face, where an AI agent swarm hacked its platform in an episode that kicked off an industry security crisis.
  • Instead, banks fear the ripple effects and risks that extend from users allowing agents to log in to their accounts and take action, especially since agents could take steps users haven't sanctioned.
  • Concerns about frontier AI systems, not AI agents, have led banks to invest in prevention and to plan for the worst.

Zoom in: The Axios report came amid growing concerns about a burgeoning cybersecurity crisis.

  • Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff posted "code red" on X, quoting an Anthropic security employee who said "as bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better."
  • The Anthropic employee was referring to security researchers finding major vulnerabilities in a programming language used to run millions of websites, marking one of the most consequential cybersecurity discoveries yet made with AI.
  • The Axios report on banks, which referred to agentic AI, not frontier AI systems, sparked calls for regulation from across the political spectrum, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.).
  • Former White House AI czar David Sacks said banks should support user-directed agents that allow users to "grant, limit, and revoke access," with read-only as an "interim step."
  • Sacks said conflating "user-authorized agentic behavior and cyberattacks is irresponsible."

Flashback: The major banks were part of early testing of Anthropic's Mythos, the most cyber-capable model from the AI company.

  • That was part of an effort from AI companies and major banks to use this technology to better understand and prepare for cyberattacks or other risks.
  • Since then, banks have worked on plans not just to avoid AI-related issues, but to protect accounts, reassure customers and keep operations running in case a large-scale attack hits.

Reality check: This is not just standard, it's required for critical industries that have to answer to the government, shareholders and customers.

  • Scenario planning is a requirement for critical infrastructure providers, including in the financial sector. Avoiding it would be malpractice.
  • The highest-risk scenarios involve fear: Speaking in Chicago earlier this month, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warned about the potential for cyberattacks or the possibility AI agents could take steps that users have not approved.
  • "You're assuming they're going to act properly on your behalf and they may not," Dimon said. The only answer is vigilance, he said, warning that stopping AI wouldn't be possible. "You can't stop it. You just have to, like, manage the hell out of it."
  • One economist last month floated the possibility of a bank run driven by agents moving the household cash of their users into higher-yield accounts.

Between the lines: Banks want customers to know they have not seen any rogue agent activity or evidence of a hack affecting customer funds or accounts.

  • Banks strongly advise users not to provide their passwords to agents, especially since services exist or are being developed that can allow customers read-only access. The startup Plaid is one such platform that can pull balances and transaction history, among other functions.
  • "Under no circumstance should customers share passwords with any person or thing. Period," a JPMorgan spokesperson told Axios. "There exist secure open banking platforms that don't involve handing over the keys to your account. Customers are the first line of defense in protecting their accounts."
  • JPMorgan has taken steps to block agent access, along with other banks, although it is exploring secure ways to allow customers to connect with the services they choose.

The intrigue: AI companies are anticipating a political backlash. Banks are preparing for potential operational disruptions.

  • The extent of federal planning for a crisis spanning both remains unclear.

The bottom line: The pace of AI advances has Wall Street and Silicon Valley preparing for worst-case scenarios while Washington is working to mitigate cyber risks and counting on voluntary safety pledges.

item.title: Why soaring prices aren't breaking America's diesel habit
item.description:
The quickest and most affordable response to historically high diesel prices is also the simplest: Use less of it.

Why it matters: Diesel is so entrenched in farming, trucking and other industries that even soaring prices aren't enough — at least not yet — to prompt a wholesale shift to alternatives from electric semi trucks to manure-powered tractors.

Catch up fast: Diesel prices have climbed to record highs since the U.S. war with Iran began in February, rising faster than gasoline amid global oil supply disruptions.

  • Diesel averaged $6.31 a gallon Thursday, up 74% from a year ago, according to AAA. Regular gasoline averaged $4.27, up 39%.

The big picture: Gasoline gets the attention, but diesel is the workhorse of the American economy. It powers grocery trucks, tractors, freight trains, construction equipment, hospital backup generators and even school buses.

Driving the news: The price spike is hitting farmers during the fall harvest.

  • "Farmers buy diesel by the truckload, so we're talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars in diesel, and when it goes up the way it has spiked, that's the difference between profit and loss in a year," said Curt Blades, senior vice president at the Association of Equipment Manufacturers, a trade group representing tractor makers and other heavy-equipment manufacturers.
  • The financial pain varies: Trucking companies can often pass higher fuel costs to customers through surcharges. Farmers, who have little control over crop prices, generally can't.

The economic pressure has become political ahead of the midterm elections.

  • President Trump announced $8 billion in one-time aid for farmers at a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, where Republicans face a competitive Senate race.
  • "It's a bit too soon to tell the impact," Blades said of the aid package, though he welcomed support during harvest.

State of play: Trucking and agricultural equipment experts say the most immediate savings come from using existing diesel engines more efficiently.

  • Truckers can slow down and reduce idling.
  • Farmers are increasingly using GPS-guided tractors to avoid covering the same ground twice, a practice known as precision agriculture.
  • Biodiesel and renewable diesel can reduce petroleum dependence without replacing existing engines, but government blending requirements — rather than high diesel prices alone — are driving growth, according to Clean Fuels Alliance America, an industry trade group.

Zoom in: Batteries that power truck drivers' sleeping quarters without idling the engine are gaining traction.

  • Nevada-based Dragonfly Energy sells systems that recharge through the truck's diesel-powered engine while driving, then power air conditioning and other appliances while parked.
  • The company projected a 160% increase in third-quarter trucking revenue, a bright spot amid otherwise sluggish financial performance.
  • Texas-based Stevens Transport says 400 of its trucks use Dragonfly's batteries, cutting diesel consumption by about 4% compared with trucks using smaller diesel engines to power their sleeping quarters.

The approach illustrates a fundamental tension in energy transitions: Does technology incrementally change an industry or revolutionize it?

  • "We haven't even mastered leaving the truck off when it's not moving, let alone moving it with electricity," said Wade Seaburg, Dragonfly's chief commercial officer. "Let's master the little things first, and that's been a well-received message."
  • "Think evolutionary rather than revolutionary," said Mike Roeth, executive director of the North American Council for Freight Efficiency, a nonprofit researching fuel-saving trucking technologies.

Zoom out: The same logic applies across diesel-dependent industries. Expensive equipment lasts for years, and switching fuels often requires new infrastructure and vehicles.

  • "The fact diesel fuel prices are higher matters in the calculations, but it doesn't make the challenges of these alternatives any easier," Roeth said.

Yes, but: More dramatic changes are still percolating, particularly in electric trucking.

  • Forum Mobility, which builds shared charging depots and leases electric trucks, says electric trucks have a roughly 40% fueling cost advantage over diesel in California, where diesel prices have topped $8 a gallon.
  • The company has commitments from 25 carriers for 330 Tesla Semis and is building four additional charging depots in California.

Meanwhile, on the farm, equipment maker New Holland has spent more than a decade bringing methane-powered tractors to market, including ones that can run on fuel made from livestock manure, after abandoning an expensive hydrogen tractor project.

  • "The increase in diesel prices has generated a little more interest," said Sean Dorosz, a product marketing manager at New Holland. But "I don't think it's going to be the one thing that makes them write a check to buy a methane tractor."
  • Access to manure-derived fuel and state incentives also shape the economics.

The bottom line: High diesel prices are strengthening the case for alternatives. Making them practical is a much slower process.

Catch up fast: Diesel prices have climbed to record highs since the U.S. war with Iran began in February, rising faster than gasoline amid global oil supply disruptions.

  • Diesel averaged $6.31 a gallon Thursday, up 74% from a year ago, according to AAA. Regular gasoline averaged $4.27, up 39%.

The big picture: Gasoline gets the attention, but diesel is the workhorse of the American economy. It powers grocery trucks, tractors, freight trains, construction equipment, hospital backup generators and even school buses.

Driving the news: The price spike is hitting farmers during the fall harvest.

  • "Farmers buy diesel by the truckload, so we're talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars in diesel, and when it goes up the way it has spiked, that's the difference between profit and loss in a year," said Curt Blades, senior vice president at the Association of Equipment Manufacturers, a trade group representing tractor makers and other heavy-equipment manufacturers.
  • The financial pain varies: Trucking companies can often pass higher fuel costs to customers through surcharges. Farmers, who have little control over crop prices, generally can't.

The economic pressure has become political ahead of the midterm elections.

  • President Trump announced $8 billion in one-time aid for farmers at a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, where Republicans face a competitive Senate race.
  • "It's a bit too soon to tell the impact," Blades said of the aid package, though he welcomed support during harvest.

State of play: Trucking and agricultural equipment experts say the most immediate savings come from using existing diesel engines more efficiently.

  • Truckers can slow down and reduce idling.
  • Farmers are increasingly using GPS-guided tractors to avoid covering the same ground twice, a practice known as precision agriculture.
  • Biodiesel and renewable diesel can reduce petroleum dependence without replacing existing engines, but government blending requirements — rather than high diesel prices alone — are driving growth, according to Clean Fuels Alliance America, an industry trade group.

Zoom in: Batteries that power truck drivers' sleeping quarters without idling the engine are gaining traction.

  • Nevada-based Dragonfly Energy sells systems that recharge through the truck's diesel-powered engine while driving, then power air conditioning and other appliances while parked.
  • The company projected a 160% increase in third-quarter trucking revenue, a bright spot amid otherwise sluggish financial performance.
  • Texas-based Stevens Transport says 400 of its trucks use Dragonfly's batteries, cutting diesel consumption by about 4% compared with trucks using smaller diesel engines to power their sleeping quarters.

The approach illustrates a fundamental tension in energy transitions: Does technology incrementally change an industry or revolutionize it?

  • "We haven't even mastered leaving the truck off when it's not moving, let alone moving it with electricity," said Wade Seaburg, Dragonfly's chief commercial officer. "Let's master the little things first, and that's been a well-received message."
  • "Think evolutionary rather than revolutionary," said Mike Roeth, executive director of the North American Council for Freight Efficiency, a nonprofit researching fuel-saving trucking technologies.

Zoom out: The same logic applies across diesel-dependent industries. Expensive equipment lasts for years, and switching fuels often requires new infrastructure and vehicles.

  • "The fact diesel fuel prices are higher matters in the calculations, but it doesn't make the challenges of these alternatives any easier," Roeth said.

Yes, but: More dramatic changes are still percolating, particularly in electric trucking.

  • Forum Mobility, which builds shared charging depots and leases electric trucks, says electric trucks have a roughly 40% fueling cost advantage over diesel in California, where diesel prices have topped $8 a gallon.
  • The company has commitments from 25 carriers for 330 Tesla Semis and is building four additional charging depots in California.

Meanwhile, on the farm, equipment maker New Holland has spent more than a decade bringing methane-powered tractors to market, including ones that can run on fuel made from livestock manure, after abandoning an expensive hydrogen tractor project.

  • "The increase in diesel prices has generated a little more interest," said Sean Dorosz, a product marketing manager at New Holland. But "I don't think it's going to be the one thing that makes them write a check to buy a methane tractor."
  • Access to manure-derived fuel and state incentives also shape the economics.

The bottom line: High diesel prices are strengthening the case for alternatives. Making them practical is a much slower process.

item.title: Airlines' new normal: Higher fares, fewer flights
item.description:
That wince you just made while researching travel options? Get used to it.

Why it matters: Soaring jet fuel prices are accelerating changes across the airline industry, seen in higher fares, premium-heavy cabins and fewer flight options for travelers.

  • Airfares rose 22% year over year in September, marking a 10th straight monthly increase in the government's airfare price index, which hit an all-time high.

State of play: All the major airlines are feeling the pain:

  • American Airlines reported Thursday that its fuel bill jumped nearly 70% in the third quarter from a year ago, adding $1.9 billion in costs and undercutting its revenue growth.
  • Southwest and United Airlines both slashed their profit forecasts this week on higher fuel costs.
  • And Delta Air Lines expects its fuel bill this year to come in $6 billion above last year's.

The impact: To protect their bottom lines, airlines are raising fares and turning to more premium seats to squeeze more revenue out of their flights.

  • At Southwest, the average passenger fare rose 26.9% to $231.69 in the third quarter, compared with a year earlier — and that doesn't include fees.
  • Delta's premium seating revenue jumped 18% in the third quarter, even though the number of premium seats rose only 6%.

What they're saying: The airlines have few options to make up for extra fuel costs other than fare increases, said Scott Keyes, founder of flight-deal service Going.com.

  • "None of them are hedging fuel the way they used to, in large part because they had a pretty terrible experience with it," Keyes said in an interview.

The big picture: Airline executives, however, see these changes — many of which were already underway — as a necessary new normal.

  • This year's fuel spike has only "accelerated" change, Delta CEO Ed Bastian said on the company's earnings call on Oct. 9.
  • "Regardless of the next move in fuel prices, the forces reshaping the U.S. airline industry will continue with many carriers struggling to earn their cost of capital well before the run-up in fuel," he said.
  • United CEO Scott Kirby told investors Wednesday that the industry's underlying costs — including airport fees, maintenance and engines — have increased so much in recent years that airlines must fundamentally change their economics.

Zoom in: Executives echoed Bastian's comments on pricing from earlier in the month, suggesting this week that the higher fares and other changes to protect profitability are likely to remain in place even after jet fuel prices ease.

  • "I'm pretty confident that we're not going to take steps backwards in pricing," Kirby said. "I think we're demonstrating this year that it's different this time."
  • American CEO Robert Isom said the fuel price spike "has just been a catalyst to allow us to realize that there is value," referring to the strong demand from customers willing to pay higher fares.

And airlines are becoming increasingly reluctant to operate flights that don't make money — potentially leaving travelers with fewer options.

  • United's Kirby predicted that trend will continue across the industry. "One golden rule — don't fly places that lose money," he said on the company's earnings call. "There's going to be less loss-making flying," he predicted.

Zoom out: The fallout from higher fuel prices — triggered largely by the war in Iran, which has throttled supplies — started with the shutdown of Spirit Airlines earlier this year.

  • While Spirit's troubles were many, the fuel price spike was widely seen as the last straw for the budget carrier.
  • And its exit means it's now easier for airlines to get away with charging more to cover their extra fuel costs, Keyes said.
  • "Spirit's demise is another factor in why you're seeing airfare go up so precipitously because they and other budget airlines act as something of an anchor for airfare in general," Keyes said.

The bottom line: Fuel prices may eventually come back down. Don't count on airfares following.

item.title: Top health adviser and MAHA ally quits Trump admin
item.description:
Calley Means, the health entrepreneur who became the Trump administration's most vocal advocate of the MAHA agenda, resigned from his senior adviser post on Thursday.

Why it matters: Means' departure two weeks before the midterm elections underscores the MAHA base's discontent with the pace of change on food policy and the administration's stances on issues like pesticide use.

Driving the news: Means expressed "tremendous respect" for President Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in a statement on X, praising their efforts to take on "entrenched, dark forces in DC" and advance the MAHA agenda.

  • He cited the administration's work to overhaul dietary guidelines, advance psychedelic therapies, ban the use of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits for sugary drinks, and get food companies to voluntarily remove artificial dyes and other additives from products.
  • The Department of Health and Human Services didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Between the lines: Tensions between the MAHA faithful and the administration peaked in February, after Trump issued an executive order to increase domestic production of glyphosate, a common weed killer.

  • Kennedy and others close to the movement had argued pesticides are making Americans sick. But agriculture interests said restricting their use would raise food prices and cost farmers billions.

Trump had tapped Means' sister, Casey, a nutrition influencer, for surgeon general last year but withdrew the nomination in April after her confirmation process stalled in the Senate.

item.title: Black October: why bugs discovered by OpenAI tech are creating a cyber emergency
item.description:
The websites you use every day may have been vulnerable to hackers for years because of hidden flaws in their code that AI only recently discovered.

Why it matters: The code, called PHP, powers millions of websites, and the vulnerabilities could allow hackers to steal sensitive data like your passwords or take control of affected servers.

Driving the news: A potential attack exploiting flaws in PHP emerged on Wednesday, which prompted governments and companies to temporarily take their websites offline while they installed security patches.

  • Dozens of websites in the U.S., U.K., and around the world were briefly taken offline to make the fix.
  • The disruption put the National Security Agency and Europe's cybersecurity agency on alert.

State of play: Security patches were released to fix the issues on Oct. 21, 2026. Cybersecurity firms urged anyone using PHP to install the security updates immediately.

What they're saying: OpenAI's technology helped find the bugs, and the company called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory."

  • "To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did," OpenAI said.
  • The cybersecurity firm Wiz wrote in a blog post: "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history."

Read more below.

What is PHP?

You've probably never heard of PHP, even though you've interacted with it for decades.

  • PHP, which stands for Hypertext Preprocessor, is a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known.
  • It has been around since the 1990s to help build websites, taking data and generating content sent to a browser.
  • It's still used today for a variety of websites, including Wikipedia, WordPress blogs and shopping websites.

How it works: HTML determines what a website displays. PHP works behind the scenes to collect information and generate content.

What was the PHP vulnerability, exactly?

AI researchers discovered two critical vulnerabilities in PHP that could allow an attacker to take control of a website's server without having legitimate access to it.

  • Hackers could exploit the flaws, dubbed "php2shell" by cybersecurity firms, to steal information from those websites.

Between the lines: The flaws went undetected for more than a decade because exploiting them required complex technical work that AI helped researchers discover, per Wiz.

Why cybersecurity incidents are a big deal

Thought bubble via Axios' Bradley Olson: The PHP vulnerabilities are so serious that the NSA warned website operators to take their sites down if they didn't have enough time to patch the bug.

  • But the cybersecurity problems in recent days have extended far beyond that and include disruptions to developer platforms, data leaks on public schools, break-ins at public companies and more.
  • A major Axios scoop also revealed that banks are detecting unauthorized third-party agent access inside customer accounts, a problem they are racing to contain.

Cyber pros are calling the series of attacks "Black October" due to the sheer volume and the level of risk, although so far many organizations have mitigated the risk and avoided massive real-world harm.

  • While defenders and AI companies have warned for months that a season of cyber emergencies would imminently arrive, they have also been working to secure some of the obscure software that still underpins much of the modern internet ecosystem.

The bottom line: As attacks continue, experts have urged users to secure passwords, use a password manager and also to avoid panic.

  • As with any cyber emergency, the true barometer of harm is the extent to which damage seeps into the real world, as it has done with ransomware that took hospital software offline or a pipeline system that disrupted fuel supplies briefly on the East Coast.

item.title: Permitting deal draws lobbying blitz as hurdles mount
item.description:
The fragile Senate permitting deal is a major priority across the energy industry, per newly filed lobbying disclosures.

Why it matters: The filings reveal behind-the-scenes efforts by powerful interests and companies representing oil and gas, mining, renewables, environmentalists and plenty in between to shape the legislation.

The big picture: The bill title (Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act), its acronym (BAAJA) and its bill number appear throughout third-quarter lobbying disclosures.

  • The bill was introduced Sept. 30, the last day of the third quarter. The disclosures, due Oct. 20, offer a window into efforts to influence the legislation during its drafting and negotiations.
  • The lobbying extends beyond groups that specifically named the bill in their filings. Many others with a stake in the bill — like the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers — list permitting legislation in other ways.

Driving the news: Here's just a small subset of the parties in the arena.

  • Industry groups like the American Petroleum Institute, the Edison Electric Institute, the American Forest & Paper Association, the National Mining Association, and the Data Center Coalition.
  • Green groups including Earthjustice, the Nature Conservancy, and Defenders of Wildlife.
  • Low-carbon power trade groups such as the Solar Energy Industries Association.

State of play: The lobbying goes far beyond trade associations, with many individual companies also involved.

  • They range from Chevron and BP to power giants like Duke Energy and Southern Company to geothermal startup Fervo.
  • Industrial and equipment heavyweights like Caterpillar, Schneider Electric and Cummins are there, too.

Zoom in: The disclosures also offer clues about which provisions attracted lobbying attention. For example:

  • The National Mining Association identified BAAJA provisions that would change Clean Water Act permitting, including state water quality reviews and limits on lawsuits challenging permits.
  • The Interstate Natural Gas Association of America listed BAAJA provisions affecting interstate natural gas pipelines among its lobbying topics, alongside other pipeline permitting proposals.

Threat level: The latest filings land amid new friction over the bill.

  • This week the Interior Department asked a federal judge to allow it to reconsider the Biden-era prior approval of Avangrid's planned New England Wind project off Massachusetts.
  • "This is how you blow up a permitting deal," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) told Axios and other outlets about the latest in a string of Trump team moves against previously approved projects.

Yes, but: An administration official cast the federal filing as a procedural move in the case brought by other opponents of the project.

  • "Our filings defend the current government's litigating position," the official said.
  • "We have been very transparent about the need for permitting reform and have also been transparent with Senator Whitehouse's and Senator [Martin] Heinrich's teams on all these legal filings," the official said, citing the two Democratic co-authors.

🆕 The latest: Democratic attorneys general from nine states express "substantial concerns" with the bill in a new letter to lawmakers, Punchbowl News reported this morning.

What we're watching: The public advocacy and closed-door maneuvering should reach a fever pitch ahead of the first procedural vote on Nov. 9, and in the days and weeks that follow.

  • The next wave of disclosures, covering October-December, should provide an even clearer look at the interests at play.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Hackers are turning web browsing into a spyware trap
item.description:
Hackers are finding new ways to infect iPhones with spyware — even when victims never click a malicious link — according to new research shared with Axios.

Why it matters: Software once used to spy on politicians, journalists and other high-value targets is becoming a tool for everyday cybercriminals looking to steal cryptocurrency and login credentials.

Driving the news: Researchers at iVerify and Report URI said Thursday they've uncovered two campaigns in which criminal groups with suspected ties to China exploited online advertising infrastructure and legitimate websites to deliver iPhone spyware.

  • In one case, iVerify found that a financial institution employee's iPhone was infected after they scrolled past a professional soccer advertisement on Instagram. The ad automatically triggered an attack that stole the person's login credentials and searched their cryptocurrency wallets.
  • In another, Report URI uncovered a campaign affecting nearly 8,000 legitimate websites after hackers purchased roughly 630 expired domains that those sites still relied on. The attackers used those domains to redirect vulnerable iPhone visitors toward spyware designed to steal their credentials and cryptocurrency.

How it works: Both campaigns exploited tools that load automatically as people browse the internet, eliminating the need to trick victims into clicking malicious links.

  • In the iVerify case, malicious code began running as soon as the Instagram advertisement appeared on the victim's screen. The attack checked the iPhone's operating system before deploying a compatible exploit.
  • In the Report URI campaign, attackers purchased expired domains once used to host legitimate website features, such as chatbots and analytics tools. Thousands of websites were still loading code from those domains, allowing criminals to quietly redirect visitors toward malicious software.

Threat level: The findings show how cybercriminals are building an infrastructure for delivering spyware through everyday online activity, rather than relying on traditional phishing attacks or targeting specific individuals.

  • Both methods also allow attackers to selectively target vulnerable devices. Advertising platforms can narrow audiences based on interests and device characteristics, while malicious website code can identify a visitor's operating system before selecting an attack.

The big picture: Cybercriminals are increasingly weaponizing spyware to exploit mobile phones, whose security (whether on an iPhone or Android) has often been seen as ironclad.

  • Last year, iVerify uncovered evidence of the first spyware campaign targeting iPhones in the U.S. and the European Union.
  • Last week, researchers at the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab uncovered the first public confirmation of zero-click spyware delivered via targeted ads — targeting at least 45 devices within international news network Al Jazeera.
  • Rocky Cole, co-founder and chief operating officer at iVerify, told Axios that spyware is now "the fastest proliferating threat to mobile devices at the current moment."

The intrigue: "They're either Chinese or they definitely want us to think that they are," Scott Helme, founder and CEO at Report URI, told Axios about the groups behind the campaigns.

What to watch: Researchers warn that the growing availability of sophisticated spyware is forcing consumers to rethink how they protect their phones.

  • Cole and Helme both emphasized keeping mobile operating systems updated, since the attacks depend on exploiting vulnerabilities in specific software versions.

item.title: Scoop: Unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts
item.description:
Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios.

Why it matters: AI agents are becoming a nightmare for America's banks, making their way into banking systems faster than financial institutions can respond.

  • The difficulty in distinguishing between a human and an unauthorized bot is forcing banks to block the technology and rapidly rewrite their terms of service.

Driving the news: Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and others are racing to contain agent risks. Some are aware of unauthorized access, people familiar with the issue said.

  • These are generally situations when an agent or AI assistant accesses a human's account with the user's permission and login credentials. Even if permitted by the user, this goes against the guidelines of most banks requiring that humans log in to their own accounts.
  • This presents significant security risks: Banking executives fear the steps agents with login access might take, especially if a user has granted purchase authority or the ability to shift funds.
  • In other instances, some banks have tracked activity when agents — programmed to fulfill requests or complete tasks on a user's behalf — contact call centers or appear to take actions independent of user instructions, the people said.

What they're saying: Bank executives described the situation as horrifying, with one official saying the industry has grave concerns about agents gaining access to customer accounts and taking steps that could impact user finances.

State of play: The concerns are at the root of the decision by several banks to restrict third-party AI agent access, the people said.

  • Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents from accessing its platforms, sources familiar with the decision said.
  • JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are also restricting agents.
  • A Chase spokesperson said customers should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone. A Morgan Stanley spokesperson said the bank hasn't observed instances of "rogue AI agents accessing our platforms."

Zoom out: Most banks have authorized or are moving in the direction of allowing read-only access, which should allow agents to see customer financial information without taking action.

  • Banks already grant such access to third-party apps like Quicken for budgeting and other activities.

Reality check: Several industry and bank executives told Axios they recognize the need to find a middle-ground with AI agents.

  • Customers will want to use these agents going forward, which banks recognize.
  • But for now, the risks of being too permissive are too high.

Threat level: Many banks are broadly not able to parse whether agent account activity is user-directed, sources said.

  • One bank executive told Axios they struggle to differentiate between agents, as well as whether an agent has been authorized by a user or has gone rogue and gained access to a customer account.

What we're watching: On one hand, banks are best positioned to respond to the threats and opportunities of AI given their cash on hand and experience as critical infrastructure.

  • But money isn't necessarily enough to solve this problem, one source said, because of how quickly the technology is developing and revealing new weaknesses in real time.
  • Banks are investing in preventing worst-case scenarios, but they are also preparing in case they do happen, including with "day after" scenario planning that would allow them to quickly secure or restore customer access, sources said.

The bottom line: The rapid pace of AI advancement is becoming a security nightmare for America's financial institutions.

item.title: AI uncovers massive flaw in web's foundational code
item.description:
Security officials are sounding the alarm over two critical vulnerabilities in a programming language used to run millions of websites, marking one of the most consequential cybersecurity discoveries yet made with AI.

Why it matters: The bugs, which researchers found partly with an OpenAI model, proves AI can uncover critical flaws humans missed for decades — raising the stakes for defenders racing to fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them at machine speed.

What they're saying: Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, a global connectivity and internet security company, said the company saw thousands of attempts to exploit the flaws in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.

  • "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X.

Driving the news: There are two problems hackers could easily exploit in an open-source programming language known as PHP that's used on nearly 70% of all websites.

  • Government officials from the U.S. to Japan are warning companies to apply a patch to fix the bugs, or consider taking down their sites to avoid an attack.
  • OpenAI touted the role its model played in discovering one of the vulnerabilities, which allowed PHP researchers to create a fix.

Between the lines: Security researchers have been skeptical of AI-generated vulnerability reports, many of which have turned out to be minor bugs or false alarms.

  • But the PHP discovery could force the cybersecurity community to reckon with the reality of AI threats.
  • "It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post Wednesday.

Threat level: If exploited, the PHP flaws would allow malicious hackers to take control of vulnerable web servers without needing a password or other credentials.

  • Since PHP runs under a wide variety of internet applications, that access could allow hackers to take over websites, steal sensitive information and tamper with a website.
  • Some website owners took their sites down earlier Wednesday, including certain services at Wikipedia and 4chan, until they had time to patch their systems.
  • "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," researchers at Wiz wrote in a post.

The big picture: AI-driven bug discoveries are shining a light on the fragility of the modern internet, which is heavily reliant on a slew of open-source software powered by volunteers.

  • The two flaws in PHP existed for decades, but demonstrated that it was possible for a hacker to exploit them required "an exceptionally complex chain of steps," researchers at Wiz added.
  • "Defenders have always relied on the gap between 'vulnerable' and 'exploitable' to buy time to patch," Michael Leland, field CTO at Island, said in an email to Axios. "That gap is rapidly closing."

What we're watching: Cybersecurity defenders are on guard for what could be a wave of incidents where websites and organizations are hacked using these two vulnerabilities in the next few weeks.

item.title: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users
item.description:
A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties Wednesday after a jury found in September that the social media giant misled users about their data privacy.

Why it matters: The penalties come nearly a decade after the Cambridge Analytica scandal first broke and signal that Big Tech can face significant financial consequences for misleading users about their privacy.

Driving the news: Judge Francis Mathew determined the penalty amount Wednesday, handing New Mexico a win as the only state to take its claims to trial after 48 others settled.

  • Mathew concluded New Mexico was entitled to $219.5 billion based on the state's maximum $5,000 penalty multiplied by 43,899,720 violations. He reduced that to $25 billion.

What they're saying: "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge."

Catch up quick: In September, a New Mexico jury said Meta had committed 43 million "willful violations" of the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act.

  • Mathew found that Facebook's privacy controls failed to give users meaningful control over their data and that third-party app developers could access their information through the platform's systems.
  • Mathew found Mark Zuckerberg knew users didn't understand how data privacy works, and exploited that, noting that the CEO had once written that users "probably don't understand their current privacy settings or care about who sees their updates."
  • Zuckerberg also wrote that the company should give users "a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don't encourage it."

Zoom out: The suit followed reporting that revealed data firm Cambridge Analytica had harvested data from more than 50 million Facebook users to craft political ads during the 2016 election.

  • After the scandal, Facebook promised more transparency, but the court found Meta failed to consistently inform users when their data was misused.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: The oil market's 2027 relief hopes are fading fast
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Traders are betting that oil prices will remain elevated for longer than they anticipated just weeks ago, threatening to prolong the inflationary pressures that businesses and consumers have weathered for months.

Why it matters: Oil inventories have helped cushion the blow from disrupted Middle Eastern supplies, but much of that buffer has been depleted since the war began.

  • The possibility of sustained price pressures into next year throws into doubt the logic that central banks traditionally rely upon to look through energy price shifts — that they represent a one-time shift in relative prices, not an ongoing inflationary process.
  • That leaves the global economy more vulnerable to another energy price surge, with potentially more lasting consequences for growth, inflation and interest rates than energy shocks of yore.

By the numbers: Oil futures for delivery in 2027 — contracts to buy or sell crude next year — have climbed to their highest levels since the Iran war began.

  • Prices for January 2027 are up 17% since early September, to more than $97 a barrel.
  • Markets still anticipate some relief next year, but considerably less than they expected just weeks ago. It's a reversal from late summer, when hopes of easing tensions with Iran and a recovery in Middle Eastern oil supplies briefly pushed futures lower.
  • June futures have jumped 18%, to $88 a barrel, while December futures are up 13%, to about $81.

State of play: Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf, including shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, surpassed prewar levels in the week ending Oct. 18, according to the Wall Street Journal. But the costly workarounds enabling that recovery have their limits.

  • Those include ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz, where security risks have deterred some vessels.
  • "You're coming up against limitations on actually how much volume you can move out of the Middle East, even with these processes," Christopher Haines, global head of oil at Energy Aspects, tells Axios.
  • Restoring confidence among shipping companies and insurers that vessels won't be attacked will be "exceptionally hard," Haines adds.

Zoom in: Economist Robin Brooks argues that oil prices reflect higher shipping costs and fears of further attacks more than actual shortages.

  • Using earlier monthly data, he estimates that Persian Gulf crude exports had recovered to 91% of prewar levels, with a "temporary fear factor" adding at least $20 a barrel.

What to watch: The Trump administration is seeking to ease fuel prices ahead of the midterms, most recently by allowing more Russian diesel onto the market.

  • But relief may be minimal: Ukrainian attacks have damaged Russian refineries, while sanctions complicate repairs, limiting additional exports, Haines says.

The bottom line: "The market narrative has shifted from "transitory" to "new normal" right before our eyes," Bob Elliot, chief investment officer at Unlimited Funds, wrote Wednesday morning.

item.title: "I am giving you money!" Nvidia's CEO wants every country to build its own AI
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is crisscrossing Europe with a multibillion-dollar checkbook and a grand ambition: Make his company the indispensable backbone of the global AI economy.

Why it matters: As fears of an AI bubble rattle Wall Street, Huang is working to spread the boom beyond the U.S. and China — courting governments, bankrolling startups and cultivating massive new markets for Nvidia's chips.

The big picture: The godfather of AI is trying to single-handedly build a new market for Nvidia chips, betting that governments and institutions around the world will want their own, highly customized data centers running open models.

  • If it works, it could shore up demand for Nvidia chips just as another big group of customers — neoclouds — appear financially shaky.

Driving the news: Part showman, part salesman, Huang has spent the past week preaching the gospel of AI across Europe ahead of a keynote Wednesday at Nvidia's flagship conference in Berlin.

  • In France, Huang announced investments in four startups and joked, whisky glass in hand, that he's "the biggest VC in Europe." President Emmanuel Macron welcomed him to Paris, while France's economy minister compared the AI revolution to the Gold Rush.
  • In Britain, Huang channeled Oprah Winfrey while announcing stakes in five startups. "I am giving you money! And I am giving you money! And I am giving you money!" he shouted from the stage of a converted London church.
  • In Sweden, Huang unveiled a supercomputer backed by the country's industrial elite, likening Nvidia's technology to a "time machine" capable of compressing years of scientific research into days.
  • In Germany, Huang challenged Chancellor Friedrich Merz to loosen Europe's regulatory instincts. "There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," he warned Monday. "Give Germany a chance. Give this industry a chance."

Zoom in: At the heart of Huang's global strategy is "sovereign AI" — the idea that every nation should build and control its own AI infrastructure, data and models, rather than depend on U.S. or Chinese tech giants.

  • In addition to roughly $10 billion in investments in Europe, Nvidia is helping build national AI ecosystems across Saudi Arabia, South Korea, India, Malaysia and Africa.
  • For Huang, the prize is a vast new class of customers, including entire countries that see AI infrastructure as an economic and national security imperative.

Between the lines: Huang's global offensive comes at a precarious moment for the AI industry, with Wall Street increasingly questioning whether the technology's enormous promise can justify its astronomical costs.

  • Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave and other "neocloud" providers have plunged, fueling fears that the companies borrowing billions to buy Nvidia's chips may struggle to pay their debts.
  • Investors are also scrutinizing a circular flow of money in which Nvidia helps finance the very companies buying its products, raising questions about how much demand is self-sustaining.

What to watch: Huang has emerged as the AI industry's chief cheerleader during periods of market turmoil, countering predictions of a bubble with assurances that demand is still accelerating.

  • His Berlin keynote offered another chance to calm investors by arguing that the next wave of AI spending will come from governments treating the technology as a national necessity, not a speculative bet.
  • Nvidia announced a number of initiatives oriented around the "AI factories" theme at the Berlin event, including a design for modular computing pods that can be quickly deployeds, and a "full-stack" option to offer "sovereign" AI solutions by combining the company's chips and a new family of open-weight models.

The bottom line: Countries racing to secure their independence in the AI age may find themselves more reliant than ever on one American company.

item.title: The permitting bill enters a critical stretch
item.description:
Data: Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy; Table: Ben Geman/Axios

The push to pass a sweeping permitting bill is gaining powerful allies and encountering fresh resistance as Congress prepares for a post-midterms showdown.

Why it matters: It's the most important energy bill in a long time.

  • Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors.
  • But some environmentalists say it badly weakens crucial protections in the name of speeding reviews.

Driving the news: A new, interactive analysis out on Wednesday projects potentially huge time savings if the bill becomes law.

  • Transmission projects could see the biggest acceleration, per Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh, a researcher with Columbia's energy think tank.
  • He based it on historical data about a large number of specific projects, then estimated how much quicker they would have proceeded under the bill.
  • Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy doesn't have an institutional position on the bill. But founding director Jason Bordoff, a prominent voice in energy policy circles, is urging environmentalists not to oppose it.

State of play: A who's who of economic and national security officials spanning six presidents (including Trump) are linking arms behind the bill in a new letter to Capitol Hill leaders.
